title: Bad breath
hookLine: angry at someone's bad breath? what can he do, it's his mouth (Meditations 5.28)

cards: Of all the things you might expect in a Roman emperor's private notebook, a note about body odor is near the bottom of the list. And yet there it is, in book five, entry twenty-eight.

He doesn't say whether he had anyone in mind. But the picture is vivid: sweaty armpits, bad breath, and someone close enough to notice, getting irritated. He uses it to think something through, and it's very practical.

teach.h: ANGRY AT BAD BREATH? WHAT GOOD IS IT?
teach.b: Are you angry with someone whose armpits smell, Marcus asks himself, or whose breath is bad? What good will that do you?

teach.h: HE HAS THE MOUTH HE HAS.
teach.b: He has the mouth he has, and the armpits he has. A smell like that has to come from things like that. A lot of small annoyances work the same way.
The loud chewer. The slow walker. The coworker who says actually before every sentence.

These come out of who they are and how they're made, not out of a plan to bother you. Then Marcus imagines an objection: but the man has reason, you'll say; he could notice and fix it. Fine, Marcus replies.

teach.h: YOU HAVE REASON TOO: TELL HIM KINDLY.
teach.b: You have reason too. So use your reasoning to stir up his. Show him.
If he listens, you'll have cured it, and there's no need for anger. And no theatrics either, he adds: not the tragic actor, and not the opposite extreme. Just calm, plain dealing.
So every small annoyance comes down to two honest options. Either it isn't theirs to change, and anger is pointless. Or it is, and a kind word works better than anger does.
Either way, anger isn't needed. And there's something warm under the joke: Marcus's answer is not to avoid the man, but to help him.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes recall Meditations 5.28 with small irritations: either it can't be helped, so let it go, or it can, so mention it kindly.

o: a small annoyance that comes from how someone is made
a warning from the body that someone is seriously ill
a sign that someone doesn't respect the people near them

games.q: it's his mouth — tap the pairs.
p: comes from the mouth he has
so do you: tell him kindly

s: Marcus says to ignore every annoying habit in silence
if it can be fixed, he says, use your reason to tell him.
this entry really is about body odor
armpits and bad breath, in the twenty-eighth entry of book five.
Marcus says anger helps people notice their faults
he says a kind word does the work, and anger isn't needed.

games.q: a friend always talks loudly on the phone in the car with you. it grates. what fits Meditations 5.28?
o: stew quietly for the whole drive.
snap at them the next time.
mention it once, kindly, or let it go.
games.why: Marcus: anger does no good. if they can change it, use your reason to stir theirs; if not, it's how they are.

practice: Bring to mind one small annoyance from someone you see often, a habit, a sound, a way of talking, and ask Marcus's question: is this something they can change? If not, say quietly, it's his mouth, or her mouth, and let it go.
If they can, picture telling them once, kindly, and see whether the anger has anything left to do.

wordCard.voice: Bad breath. Marcus asks what good anger does at someone's smell: he has the mouth he has. If it can be fixed, tell him kindly. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'reason, word': Marcus says you both have it, so use yours to stir his, not to rage.

carryVoice: Your line: it's his mouth. Either way, anger has nothing left to do. Back tomorrow.
